PAGE 1: How we will learn

OVERVIEW
========

Sanatan and Vedic teaching offers principles that shape a good life. This sub-strand studies five of them: Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana. You will learn what each word means, meet it in a moral story, and practise it in the way you treat people, work and prayer.

## Strand 7.0: Principles of Dharma
Sub-strand 7.1: Virtues for righteousness
Suggested lessons: 10

## What this sub-strand covers
• Sanatan/Vedic based on moral stories
• Paramatma
• Purushartha
• Pranidaya
• Punarjanam
• Prarthana

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Hindu Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 7.0 Principles of Dharma, Sub-strand 7.1 Virtues for righteousness

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation
b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living
c) appreciate the Principles of Dharma in building up one’s character

## Key inquiry questions
1. How do the Principles of Dharma relate to your daily life?

## Learning experiences
• narrate stories on Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic
• perform skits depicting Principles of Dharma
• download and read the Principles of Dharma using digital devices
• visit Sanatan/Hindu temple to learn more about Principles of Dharma and share their knowledge in class
• observe and practise the Principles of Dharma depicted in stories from Scriptures
• assist learners with special needs as per their abilities through peer teaching to make them understand the lessons drawn from the short stories

## Core competencies
• Learning to learn: Learner develops independent learning when visiting Sanatan/Hindu temple to learn more about the Principles of Dharma and sharing their knowledge in class.
• Digital Literacy: Learner enhances interacting with digital technology when downloading and reading the Principles of Dharma using digital devices.

## Values
• Peace: Learner inculcates compassion and responsibility when narrating stories on the Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Learner Support Programmes (LSPs): Learner develops positive discipline when observing and practising the Principles of Dharma depicted in stories from Scriptures.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learner is able to link the skills of performing skits depicting Principles of Dharma to the creative skills learnt in Creative Arts.

PAGE 2: Lesson 1: Five principles of dharma — How the set holds together

LESSON 1: FIVE PRINCIPLES OF DHARMA
===================================

## What you will learn
• Say what dharma means in this lesson.
• Name the five selected principles: Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation

## Introduction
Rules on a classroom wall are easy to point at. Dharma is deeper: it is the right way of living, the duty that keeps a person and a community in order. Sanatan teaching gathers that way of living into great principles.

## Notes

### Dharma
Dharma means righteousness and duty. It includes what you owe to your family, to other people, to living beings and to Paramatma. A virtue is a good quality that has become part of you, not a costume you wear for one lesson. This sub-strand is called virtues for righteousness because the principles are meant to build character.

### The five to identify
Learn these names until you can say them without the book:
- **Paramatma** — the Supreme Being, God
- **Purushartha** — the rightful aims of a human life
- **Pranidaya** — mercy and kindness towards living beings
- **Punarjanam** — birth again; the teaching that the soul's journey continues and that actions matter
- **Prarthana** — prayer

They are a set. Leaving one out means the list is not yet complete. Mixing in other good words, such as the names of festivals, does not help. Those belong to other sub-strands.

### How the set holds together
Paramatma is the One you worship. Purushartha tells you which aims are worth chasing. Pranidaya tells you how to treat living beings while you chase them. Punarjanam tells you that today's kindness or cruelty is not meaningless. Prarthana is the daily conversation with God that keeps the other four awake.

You will not finish a whole life of dharma in Grade 4. You will become familiar with the five names and use them in small, true actions. Familiarity that never changes behaviour is only spelling. The later lessons turn each word into a practice.

PAGE 3: Lesson 1: Five principles of dharma — Five name cards

## Key words
• dharma — righteousness and rightful duty
• virtue — a good quality practised until it becomes part of character
• principle — a basic truth that guides actions

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner lists Paramatma, Diwali, Purushartha, yoga and prasad. Which names from the five principles are missing, and which extras do not belong?

Working:
1. Paramatma and Purushartha are correctly included.
2. Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana are missing.
3. Diwali, yoga and prasad are not the five principles of this sub-strand.

Answer: Add Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana. Remove Diwali, yoga and prasad from this list.

## Activity: Five name cards
You will need: Five cards, A chart

1. Write one principle on each card.

2. As a class, put the cards in the order Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam, Prarthana and say each word aloud.

3. Under each card, leave space for a meaning you will complete in later lessons.

4. Help a classmate who needs the words read by pointing to each card as the class says it.

## Practice

1. What is dharma?

2. Name the five selected principles in this sub-strand.

3. Which principle means prayer?

## Answers to practice

1. Righteousness and rightful duty.

2. Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana.

3. Prarthana.

## Summary
• Dharma is righteous duty.
• The five principles are Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana.
• The set links God, rightful aims, kindness, the weight of actions, and prayer.

PAGE 4: Lesson 2: Paramatma, the Supreme Being — A story of seeing truly

LESSON 2: PARAMATMA, THE SUPREME BEING
======================================

## What you will learn
• Explain the meaning of Paramatma.
• Show one way of treating other people as belonging to God.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation; b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living

## Introduction
Paramatma is not a person in the next classroom. The word names the Supreme Soul, God, who Sanatan teaching says is present in all places and is the source of every life. How you treat people is tied to how you think about God.

## Notes

### The word
Parama means supreme. Atma means soul or self. Paramatma is the Supreme Self. In worship you may also say Bhagwan, Ishwar or other names your family uses. This lesson uses Paramatma because that is the principle on the syllabus. Different names do not mean different rival gods in this teaching. They are ways of speaking to the One.

### A story of seeing truly
Prahlad, whom you may already know, would not call a proud king Paramatma. He trusted Vishnu even when the king was stronger. Another gentle teaching story used with children is this: a host who honours a hungry guest honours more than a stranger, because the guest is received as God's visitor. You do not need a new miracle to practise the point. You need clear sight. The classmate you are tempted to insult is not rubbish. They are a living person.

PAGE 5: Lesson 2: Paramatma, the Supreme Being — Apply it

### Apply it
- Speak about God with respect, and do not use holy names as swear words.
- Do not bully. If Paramatma is the Lord of all, then bullying is an attack on someone God values.
- Serve a visitor at home with water and a seat before you think of showing off your toys.
- When you pray, you are turning towards Paramatma, not towards your own pride.

Appreciation of this principle grows when worship and behaviour match. A person who sings about God and then mocks a poorer child has split the principle in two. Join it together again by a kind action the same day.

## Key words
• Paramatma — the Supreme Soul; God
• atma — the self or soul

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner says, 'Paramatma only cares about people who look like my family.' How does the meaning of Paramatma answer that?

Working:
1. Paramatma means the Supreme Being, not the mascot of one group.
2. Sanatan teaching speaks of God as present in all life.
3. The practical result is respect for people who are different from you.

Answer: Paramatma is the God of all, so people outside your family are also to be treated with respect.

PAGE 6: Lesson 3: Purushartha, the aims of life

## Activity: A story about Paramatma
You will need: Exercise book

1. Listen to a short Sanatan story your teacher chooses about faith in God or about honouring a guest.

2. Write the meaning of Paramatma in your own words.

3. Name one school action that follows from the principle, such as refusing to bully.

4. Share the action in a group and listen to other learners without mocking their family names for God.

## Practice

1. What does Paramatma mean?

2. Give one action at school that fits this principle.

3. Why is it wrong to use a name of God as a swear word?

## Answers to practice

1. The Supreme Soul, or God.

2. Any one: refusing to bully, speaking of God respectfully, or welcoming a new classmate.

3. The principle teaches reverence for Paramatma, not careless or insulting speech.

## Summary
• Paramatma means the Supreme Soul, God.
• Respect for God shows up as respect for people.
• Holy names are not to be used as insults.

LESSON 3: PURUSHARTHA, THE AIMS OF LIFE
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Name the four aims inside Purushartha: dharma, artha, kama and moksha.
• Explain how dharma should guide money and wishes.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation; b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living

## Introduction
People want many things: to do right, to have enough, to enjoy a game or a song, and to be free from selfishness. Sanatan teaching does not pretend humans have no aims. It gathers rightful aims under the name Purushartha and puts them in order.

## Notes

### Four aims
Purushartha means the aims of a human being. The four classical aims are:
- **Dharma** — righteous duty
- **Artha** — material need: food, shelter, and money earned fairly
- **Kama** — rightful enjoyment, such as friendship, art, play and, later in life, family affection
- **Moksha** — liberation, freedom from selfish bondage, living close to Paramatma

For Grade 4, kama is not a lesson about adult matters. It means good and proper joys: a fair game, music, a meal with your family. Anything that harms you or another person is not rightful kama.

PAGE 7: Lesson 3: Purushartha, the aims of life — Dharma first

### Dharma first
Artha without dharma becomes greed. A wish without dharma becomes grabbing. Even the hope of moksha is not an excuse to neglect homework or to be cruel on the way. Dharma guides the other aims. That is why a stolen sweet is not a rightful enjoyment, and a profit made by cheating a classmate is not rightful artha.

### A story shape
Think of a market seller who gives correct measure and still earns a living. The seller has artha, but dharma decides the measure. Think of King Harishchandra, who would not drop truth to get his comfort back. Comfort is an aim. Truth is the guide.

### Your aims this term
You can want good marks (a kind of artha of effort), enjoy games (kama in a child's form), and still refuse to cheat (dharma). You can remember Paramatma at the end of the day (a step towards moksha, not a claim that you have finished the journey). Write your aims down. Cross out any aim that needs a lie.

## Key words
• Purushartha — the rightful aims of human life
• artha — material well-being and fairly earned wealth
• moksha — liberation; freedom from selfish bondage

PAGE 8: Lesson 3: Purushartha, the aims of life — Example 1

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these aims: cheating to get money, playing a fair game, doing your class duty, remembering God. Which aim is not a rightful purushartha?

Working:
1. Class duty is dharma.
2. A fair game can be rightful enjoyment.
3. Remembering God looks towards moksha.
4. Cheating for money spoils artha because dharma is missing.

Answer: Cheating to get money is not a rightful aim.

## Activity: Four aims on a chart
You will need: A four-column chart

1. Head the columns Dharma, Artha, Kama and Moksha.

2. Under each, write one example that is right for a Grade 4 learner.

3. Cross-check the kama column so that it contains only proper joys, such as play or music.

4. Discuss how dharma guides the wish to have money.

## Practice

1. What is Purushartha?

2. Name the four aims.

3. Why is money earned by cheating not true artha?

## Answers to practice

1. The rightful aims of a human life.

2. Dharma, artha, kama and moksha.

3. Artha should be guided by dharma. Cheating breaks righteousness.

## Summary
• Purushartha includes dharma, artha, kama and moksha.
• Dharma must guide money and enjoyment.
• Children's rightful joys are things such as fair play, arts and family life, not harm.

PAGE 9: Lesson 4: Pranidaya, kindness to living beings — A story of refuge

LESSON 4: PRANIDAYA, KINDNESS TO LIVING BEINGS
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain Pranidaya as compassion for every living being.
• Apply it to animals, plants and people at school.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation; b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living

## Introduction
A living being does not have to be your friend before you refuse to harm it. Pranidaya joins two ideas: prani, a living being, and daya, mercy or compassion. It is kindness that notices life.

## Notes

### The meaning
The syllabus spells this principle Pranidaya. In this lesson it means daya, mercy, shown to every prani, every living being. People, animals and even the plants you studied as sacred are included. Compassion is not softness that ignores danger. You may step away from a snake and call an adult. You may not throw stones at the snake for fun.

### A story of refuge
A well-known moral story tells of King Shibi. A dove sought refuge with him, and a hawk demanded the dove as food. The king would not betray the bird that had trusted him. He offered his own flesh to match the dove's weight rather than break mercy. You are not asked to copy the injury. You are asked to copy the choice: a creature that comes to you for safety should not be handed to cruelty. In school, that may be a classmate hiding from bullies, or a bird that has fallen in the compound. Call an adult. Do not join the harm.

### Daily forms
- Do not hit animals or tear leaves off a living tree for sport.
- Share food with someone who has none, without making them feel small.
- Speak gently to a learner who is slow, afraid or new.
- If you keep a pet, give it water and do not neglect it.
- When you plant a seedling, you are also practising care for living things.

Peace in a class often begins with this principle. Cruel jokes are a failure of daya. A repaired friendship is a sign that mercy has done some work.

PAGE 10: Lesson 4: Pranidaya, kindness to living beings — Example 1

## Key words
• Pranidaya — compassion and mercy towards living beings
• daya — mercy or compassion
• prani — a living being

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Learners corner a frightened cat and laugh. Which principle is being broken, and what should a watcher do?

Working:
1. The cat is a prani. Cornering it for fun breaks Pranidaya.
2. The watcher should refuse to join in.
3. They should ask an adult to help the animal safely, not start a new attack.

Answer: Pranidaya is broken. Stop the teasing and get an adult to help.

## Activity: Skit of mercy
You will need: Space to act

1. In groups, act a short skit: a dove, or a classmate, asks for refuge, and the group chooses mercy instead of mockery.

2. Do not act injury. End with a safe, kind action.

3. Name the principle: Pranidaya.

4. Write one way you will show daya to a living being this week.

## Practice

1. What does Pranidaya mean in this lesson?

2. What choice does the story of King Shibi praise?

3. Give one way to practise Pranidaya at school.

## Answers to practice

1. Compassion or mercy shown to living beings.

2. He protected the dove that took refuge with him instead of giving it up to harm.

3. Any one: do not harm animals, do not mock a frightened classmate, speak gently, or care for a plant.

## Summary
• Pranidaya means mercy towards living beings.
• The story of King Shibi and the dove teaches refuge, not a dare to get hurt.
• School practice includes protecting animals and speaking kindly.

PAGE 11: Lesson 5: Punarjanam and the weight of actions

LESSON 5: PUNARJANAM AND THE WEIGHT OF ACTIONS
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain Punarjanam in simple, careful words.
• Show how good and harmful actions shape character now.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation; b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living

## Introduction
Punarjanam means birth again. Sanatan teaching says the soul does not finish its journey in a single lifetime, and that actions, called karma, matter. The point for a child is not to be frightened. The point is to choose good actions today.

## Notes

### The words
Punar means again. Janam means birth. Punarjanam is the teaching of rebirth. Karma means action, and also the moral weight actions carry. You are not asked to describe other people's past lives. You cannot see that, and guessing it is unkind. 'He is poor because of a past life' is a sentence this lesson forbids. It can be used to excuse meanness. Dharma tells you to help a person in need now.

PAGE 12: Lesson 5: Punarjanam and the weight of actions — What you can know

### What you can know
You can know that habits grow. A learner who tells the truth finds it easier to tell the truth next time. A learner who mocks others becomes quicker to mock. Character is built, or spoiled, by repetition. Punarjanam extends that seriousness: Sanatan teaching says the soul carries the fruit of actions beyond what we can see in one term. Even if a classmate from another faith does not share the whole teaching, the shared moral is clear. What we do matters.

### Stories without scary detail
Scripture is full of people who met the fruit of pride and of people who were protected for their goodness. You already know Prahlad's faith and the fall of a cruel king. Use those stories to talk about justice and mercy, not to invent punishments for your enemies.

### Apply it
Before a harsh act, pause and ask: 'If this action shapes me, do I want that shape?' Then choose the kinder action. Apologise when you have been wrong, because repair is also karma of a good kind. Do not threaten a classmate with rebirth. That is bullying dressed up as religion.

Appreciate the principle as a call to responsibility. It makes ordinary kindness important.

## Key words
• Punarjanam — rebirth; the teaching that the soul is born again
• karma — action, and the moral result that actions bring

PAGE 13: Lesson 5: Punarjanam and the weight of actions — Answers to practice

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Someone says a classmate deserves unkindness because of punarjanam. What is the right reply?

Working:
1. You cannot know another person's unseen story.
2. Using the idea as an excuse to be cruel breaks dharma and Pranidaya.
3. The right use of the teaching is to watch your own actions.

Answer: Refuse the unkindness. Punarjanam is not a reason to hurt someone. It is a reason to choose good actions yourself.

## Activity: Actions that shape us
You will need: Two columns on paper

1. Head the columns 'Actions that build good character' and 'Actions that spoil it'.

2. List school examples in each column. Do not write classmates' names in the unkind column.

3. Discuss the meaning of Punarjanam without guessing anyone's past life.

4. Each learner writes one action they will repeat this week because it builds the character they want.

## Practice

1. What does Punarjanam mean?

2. What is karma in this lesson?

3. Why must you not blame a classmate's hardship on a past life?

## Answers to practice

1. Birth again; the teaching that the soul continues and is born again.

2. Action, and the moral weight or result that actions carry.

3. You cannot know that, and the idea must not be used to excuse unkindness. Dharma says to help.

## Summary
• Punarjanam means rebirth in Sanatan teaching.
• Karma means that actions matter and shape us.
• The teaching is not an excuse to be cruel or to guess another person's past.

LESSON 6: PRARTHANA, PRAYER THAT CHANGES THE DAY
================================================

## What you will learn
• Explain Prarthana as one of the five principles.
• Pray, or sit respectfully, in a way that includes thanks and a promise to do right.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation; b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living

## Introduction
You have already learned set prayers such as the Gayatri and Saraswati Vandana. Here prayer returns as a principle of dharma. Prarthana is not an extra hobby. It is one of the five supports of a righteous life.

PAGE 14: Lesson 6: Prarthana, prayer that changes the day — Manners

## Notes

### What this principle adds
Prarthana means prayer. As a principle of dharma it says that a good life stays in conversation with Paramatma. Prayer can thank, praise, ask for a clean heart, or admit a fault. Asking only for prizes, while refusing to change, is a thin kind of prayer.

A useful pattern for a child has three parts:
- **Thanks** — for parents, food, a new day, a friend
- **Sorry** — for a named fault, without hiding it
- **Please** — for courage to do one right action today

You may use the prayers of your own family. A learner from another home can sit quietly and respectfully while Sanatan classmates recite, and can still write the three-part pattern in their own words.

### Prayer and effort
Purushartha includes effort. Prarthana does not cancel effort. You pray, and you also revise. You pray, and you also apologise to the person you hurt. Scripture praises people who remembered God and then did the duty in front of them.

### Manners
Pray in a clean, quiet corner if you can. Do not shove. Do not laugh at a posture of prayer you do not use at home. If the class recites a prayer you have been taught, join sincerely or remain silent and still. Both can be respectful. Whispering jokes during a prayer breaks the principle you are studying.

The link with the other principles is simple. In prayer you turn to Paramatma, you ask for dharma to guide your aims, you ask for daya, and you ask for strength to choose good actions.

PAGE 15: Lesson 6: Prarthana, prayer that changes the day — A three-part prayer

## Key words
• Prarthana — prayer; speaking with God

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner prays to pass a test and then copies the answers. Which part of the principle was missed?

Working:
1. Prayer was used like a shortcut.
2. Dharma and honest purushartha were ignored.
3. A fitting prayer would ask for a clear mind and would be followed by real revision and honest writing.

Answer: The learner separated prayer from right action. Prayer should be followed by honest effort.

## Activity: A three-part prayer
You will need: Exercise book, A quiet moment

1. Write three lines beginning Thank you, I am sorry, and Please help me to do one right action.

2. If the class recites a known prayer such as the Gayatri or Saraswati Vandana, do so respectfully. Learners who do not recite sit quietly.

3. Share only the 'please' line if you want to, not a private 'sorry' that names other children.

4. Visit is not required today. If you later visit a mandir, remember this principle and observe the rites you have been taught.

PAGE 16: Lesson 7: Stories that carry the principles

## Practice

1. What is Prarthana?

2. Name the three parts of the simple prayer pattern in this lesson.

3. Why is praying and then cheating a failure of this principle?

## Answers to practice

1. Prayer.

2. Thanks, sorry, and please help me to do what is right.

3. Prarthana is meant to turn a person towards God and towards right action, not to excuse a wrong act.

## Summary
• Prarthana is prayer, one of the five principles.
• A simple pattern is thanks, sorry and a request for help to do right.
• Prayer works together with effort and honesty.

LESSON 7: STORIES THAT CARRY THE PRINCIPLES
===========================================

## What you will learn
• Match a moral story to the principle it teaches.
• Explain how stories build character when they are retold accurately.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation; c) appreciate the Principles of Dharma in building up one’s character

## Introduction
Principles can sound like a word list until a story gives them legs. Sanatan and Vedic tradition teaches through stories. The skill is to know which principle a story is carrying, and not to twist the story into something it did not say.

PAGE 17: Lesson 7: Stories that carry the principles — Matches you can defend

## Notes

### Matches you can defend
- **Prahlad and Narsimha** carry Paramatma: God is the one to worship, and God protects a faithful person. They also warn against pride.
- **A fair seller, or Harishchandra's love of truth**, carries Purushartha: rightful aims stay under dharma.
- **King Shibi and the dove** carries Pranidaya: mercy to a living being that seeks refuge.
- **The repeated truth about habits** carries Punarjanam carefully: actions shape a person, and Sanatan teaching says their weight continues. Do not add a made-up past life.
- **A child who prays and then does the chore** carries Prarthana joined to effort.

If you tell these stories in a skit, keep the match. A skit that turns Shibi into a bully has lost the principle. A skit that uses Punarjanam to mock a classmate has become cruel.

### Character
Character is what you are when the skit is over. Stories build it when you admire the right action and repeat a piece of it. They fail when you only enjoy the costume. Appreciation of the principles means you want a character that is reverent, fair, merciful, responsible and prayerful.

### At the mandir or at home
If you visit a Sanatan temple, you may see pictures of these stories on a wall. Ask a parent or priest what the picture teaches. Share the answer in class in your own words. Do not invent a label for a picture you do not know. A digital reading, if the teacher downloads a text, should be a source you can name, not a page of unkind comments.

PAGE 18: Lesson 7: Stories that carry the principles — Match stories to principles

## Key words
• character — the moral qualities that show what a person is really like

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A group acts King Shibi throwing the dove to the hawk, and they call it Pranidaya. What is wrong?

Working:
1. The story's mercy is the protection of the dove.
2. Throwing the dove away reverses the teaching.
3. The skit should be redone so that refuge is honoured.

Answer: The skit teaches the opposite of Pranidaya and should be corrected.

## Activity: Match stories to principles
You will need: Story cards, Principle cards

1. Match each story you have learned to Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam or Prarthana.

2. Perform one corrected skit that keeps the true lesson.

3. After the skit, say how the story could build character in your class.

4. Help a learner who needs the matching done orally.

## Practice

1. Which principle is taught by the story of King Shibi and the dove?

2. Which principle is clearest in Prahlad's refusal to worship a proud king as God?

3. How can a story build character rather than only entertain?

## Answers to practice

1. Pranidaya, compassion for a living being.

2. Paramatma.

3. When the listener copies the right action, such as telling the truth or showing mercy.

## Summary
• Each principle can be carried by a true story.
• A skit must not reverse mercy or invent someone's past life.
• Stories build character when the right action is copied in real life.

LESSON 8: BUILDING CHARACTER DAY BY DAY
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Apply all five principles to one school day.
• Explain why character is built by repeated choices.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living; c) appreciate the Principles of Dharma in building up one’s character

## Introduction
Knowing five names is the start. A harmonious life is the aim. This lesson walks through one ordinary day and asks where Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana can actually appear.

PAGE 19: Lesson 8: Building character day by day — A day mapped to the five

## Notes

### A day mapped to the five
- **Morning prarthana:** thank Paramatma, and ask for a clean heart.
- **On the way to school:** show Pranidaya. Do not throw stones at animals. Help a smaller child cross safely if a known adult has asked you to walk together.
- **In class:** let dharma guide purushartha. Do your own work. Enjoy break without cheating at games.
- **When you are angry:** remember that actions shape you. A cruel reply is a seed you will meet again in your own habits. Choose repair instead.
- **Evening:** pray again, naming one good act and one act you will improve. That honesty is character under construction.

### Harmony
Harmonious living means people can share a room, a home and a road without fear of mockery or cheating. The five principles serve that peace. A class that prays and then bullies is not harmonious. A class that is kind but never tells the truth is not harmonious either. Dharma holds the pieces together.

### Appreciation
Write a short paragraph that begins, 'I appreciate these principles because...' Give a real reason: they stop you treating people as tools, they put money under honesty, they make prayer practical. Read it only if you wish. Appreciation that is copied from a neighbour without thought is thin.

PAGE 20: Lesson 8: Building character day by day — My five-principle day

### Keep going
Choose one principle that is weakest in you and one action for the next seven days. Tell a parent. If you fail on Tuesday, continue on Wednesday. Character is repetition, not a single perfect morning. When you next visit a mandir or sit with a grandparent, ask them which of the five they think a child should practise first, and listen.

## Key words
• harmonious — living together in fairness, peace and respect
• character — the kind of person your repeated choices are making

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During one afternoon a learner cheats in a game, laughs at a bird, and refuses to pray because 'principles are only for the exercise book'. Which principles need repair?

Working:
1. Cheating breaks dharma inside Purushartha.
2. Laughing at the bird breaks Pranidaya.
3. Refusing even a moment of respect breaks the daily place of Prarthana. All three can be repaired by an apology and a different choice.

Answer: Purushartha guided by dharma, Pranidaya and Prarthana.

## Activity: My five-principle day
You will need: Exercise book

1. Draw a simple day from morning to evening.

2. Write one action beside each of the five principles.

3. Share the plan in a group and correct any action that contradicts the principle.

4. Peer-teach the five names to a classmate who was away, using your day plan as the examples.

## Practice

1. Give one morning action and one class action that apply the principles.

2. Why is a single good morning not yet a full character?

3. How do the five principles help people live together harmoniously?

## Answers to practice

1. Morning: a short prayer of thanks. Class: doing your own work, or another true pair.

2. Character is built by repeating right choices, including starting again after a failure.

3. They teach reverence, fair aims, mercy, responsibility for actions and prayer, which reduce bullying and cheating.

## Summary
• Each part of the day can carry one of the five principles.
• Harmony needs honesty and kindness together.
• Character grows when a chosen action is repeated, including after a failure.

studyPages.title: How we will learn
studyPages.body:
OVERVIEW
========

Sanatan and Vedic teaching offers principles that shape a good life. This sub-strand studies five of them: Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana. You will learn what each word means, meet it in a moral story, and practise it in the way you treat people, work and prayer.

## Strand 7.0: Principles of Dharma
Sub-strand 7.1: Virtues for righteousness
Suggested lessons: 10

## What this sub-strand covers
• Sanatan/Vedic based on moral stories
• Paramatma
• Purushartha
• Pranidaya
• Punarjanam
• Prarthana

## Source
• KICD Grade 4 Hindu Religious Education Curriculum Design (Revised 2024) — Strand 7.0 Principles of Dharma, Sub-strand 7.1 Virtues for righteousness

## Learning outcomes
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation
b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living
c) appreciate the Principles of Dharma in building up one’s character

## Key inquiry questions
1. How do the Principles of Dharma relate to your daily life?

## Learning experiences
• narrate stories on Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic
• perform skits depicting Principles of Dharma
• download and read the Principles of Dharma using digital devices
• visit Sanatan/Hindu temple to learn more about Principles of Dharma and share their knowledge in class
• observe and practise the Principles of Dharma depicted in stories from Scriptures
• assist learners with special needs as per their abilities through peer teaching to make them understand the lessons drawn from the short stories

## Core competencies
• Learning to learn: Learner develops independent learning when visiting Sanatan/Hindu temple to learn more about the Principles of Dharma and sharing their knowledge in class.
• Digital Literacy: Learner enhances interacting with digital technology when downloading and reading the Principles of Dharma using digital devices.

## Values
• Peace: Learner inculcates compassion and responsibility when narrating stories on the Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic.

## Pertinent and contemporary issues
• Learner Support Programmes (LSPs): Learner develops positive discipline when observing and practising the Principles of Dharma depicted in stories from Scriptures.

## Links to other learning areas
• Learner is able to link the skills of performing skits depicting Principles of Dharma to the creative skills learnt in Creative Arts.

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Five principles of dharma — How the set holds together
studyPages.body:
LESSON 1: FIVE PRINCIPLES OF DHARMA
===================================

## What you will learn
• Say what dharma means in this lesson.
• Name the five selected principles: Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation

## Introduction
Rules on a classroom wall are easy to point at. Dharma is deeper: it is the right way of living, the duty that keeps a person and a community in order. Sanatan teaching gathers that way of living into great principles.

## Notes

### Dharma
Dharma means righteousness and duty. It includes what you owe to your family, to other people, to living beings and to Paramatma. A virtue is a good quality that has become part of you, not a costume you wear for one lesson. This sub-strand is called virtues for righteousness because the principles are meant to build character.

### The five to identify
Learn these names until you can say them without the book:
- **Paramatma** — the Supreme Being, God
- **Purushartha** — the rightful aims of a human life
- **Pranidaya** — mercy and kindness towards living beings
- **Punarjanam** — birth again; the teaching that the soul's journey continues and that actions matter
- **Prarthana** — prayer

They are a set. Leaving one out means the list is not yet complete. Mixing in other good words, such as the names of festivals, does not help. Those belong to other sub-strands.

### How the set holds together
Paramatma is the One you worship. Purushartha tells you which aims are worth chasing. Pranidaya tells you how to treat living beings while you chase them. Punarjanam tells you that today's kindness or cruelty is not meaningless. Prarthana is the daily conversation with God that keeps the other four awake.

You will not finish a whole life of dharma in Grade 4. You will become familiar with the five names and use them in small, true actions. Familiarity that never changes behaviour is only spelling. The later lessons turn each word into a practice.

studyPages.title: Lesson 1: Five principles of dharma — Five name cards
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• dharma — righteousness and rightful duty
• virtue — a good quality practised until it becomes part of character
• principle — a basic truth that guides actions

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner lists Paramatma, Diwali, Purushartha, yoga and prasad. Which names from the five principles are missing, and which extras do not belong?

Working:
1. Paramatma and Purushartha are correctly included.
2. Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana are missing.
3. Diwali, yoga and prasad are not the five principles of this sub-strand.

Answer: Add Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana. Remove Diwali, yoga and prasad from this list.

## Activity: Five name cards
You will need: Five cards, A chart

1. Write one principle on each card.

2. As a class, put the cards in the order Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam, Prarthana and say each word aloud.

3. Under each card, leave space for a meaning you will complete in later lessons.

4. Help a classmate who needs the words read by pointing to each card as the class says it.

## Practice

1. What is dharma?

2. Name the five selected principles in this sub-strand.

3. Which principle means prayer?

## Answers to practice

1. Righteousness and rightful duty.

2. Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana.

3. Prarthana.

## Summary
• Dharma is righteous duty.
• The five principles are Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana.
• The set links God, rightful aims, kindness, the weight of actions, and prayer.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Paramatma, the Supreme Being — A story of seeing truly
studyPages.body:
LESSON 2: PARAMATMA, THE SUPREME BEING
======================================

## What you will learn
• Explain the meaning of Paramatma.
• Show one way of treating other people as belonging to God.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation; b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living

## Introduction
Paramatma is not a person in the next classroom. The word names the Supreme Soul, God, who Sanatan teaching says is present in all places and is the source of every life. How you treat people is tied to how you think about God.

## Notes

### The word
Parama means supreme. Atma means soul or self. Paramatma is the Supreme Self. In worship you may also say Bhagwan, Ishwar or other names your family uses. This lesson uses Paramatma because that is the principle on the syllabus. Different names do not mean different rival gods in this teaching. They are ways of speaking to the One.

### A story of seeing truly
Prahlad, whom you may already know, would not call a proud king Paramatma. He trusted Vishnu even when the king was stronger. Another gentle teaching story used with children is this: a host who honours a hungry guest honours more than a stranger, because the guest is received as God's visitor. You do not need a new miracle to practise the point. You need clear sight. The classmate you are tempted to insult is not rubbish. They are a living person.

studyPages.title: Lesson 2: Paramatma, the Supreme Being — Apply it
studyPages.body:
### Apply it
- Speak about God with respect, and do not use holy names as swear words.
- Do not bully. If Paramatma is the Lord of all, then bullying is an attack on someone God values.
- Serve a visitor at home with water and a seat before you think of showing off your toys.
- When you pray, you are turning towards Paramatma, not towards your own pride.

Appreciation of this principle grows when worship and behaviour match. A person who sings about God and then mocks a poorer child has split the principle in two. Join it together again by a kind action the same day.

## Key words
• Paramatma — the Supreme Soul; God
• atma — the self or soul

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner says, 'Paramatma only cares about people who look like my family.' How does the meaning of Paramatma answer that?

Working:
1. Paramatma means the Supreme Being, not the mascot of one group.
2. Sanatan teaching speaks of God as present in all life.
3. The practical result is respect for people who are different from you.

Answer: Paramatma is the God of all, so people outside your family are also to be treated with respect.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Purushartha, the aims of life
studyPages.body:
## Activity: A story about Paramatma
You will need: Exercise book

1. Listen to a short Sanatan story your teacher chooses about faith in God or about honouring a guest.

2. Write the meaning of Paramatma in your own words.

3. Name one school action that follows from the principle, such as refusing to bully.

4. Share the action in a group and listen to other learners without mocking their family names for God.

## Practice

1. What does Paramatma mean?

2. Give one action at school that fits this principle.

3. Why is it wrong to use a name of God as a swear word?

## Answers to practice

1. The Supreme Soul, or God.

2. Any one: refusing to bully, speaking of God respectfully, or welcoming a new classmate.

3. The principle teaches reverence for Paramatma, not careless or insulting speech.

## Summary
• Paramatma means the Supreme Soul, God.
• Respect for God shows up as respect for people.
• Holy names are not to be used as insults.

LESSON 3: PURUSHARTHA, THE AIMS OF LIFE
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Name the four aims inside Purushartha: dharma, artha, kama and moksha.
• Explain how dharma should guide money and wishes.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation; b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living

## Introduction
People want many things: to do right, to have enough, to enjoy a game or a song, and to be free from selfishness. Sanatan teaching does not pretend humans have no aims. It gathers rightful aims under the name Purushartha and puts them in order.

## Notes

### Four aims
Purushartha means the aims of a human being. The four classical aims are:
- **Dharma** — righteous duty
- **Artha** — material need: food, shelter, and money earned fairly
- **Kama** — rightful enjoyment, such as friendship, art, play and, later in life, family affection
- **Moksha** — liberation, freedom from selfish bondage, living close to Paramatma

For Grade 4, kama is not a lesson about adult matters. It means good and proper joys: a fair game, music, a meal with your family. Anything that harms you or another person is not rightful kama.

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Purushartha, the aims of life — Dharma first
studyPages.body:
### Dharma first
Artha without dharma becomes greed. A wish without dharma becomes grabbing. Even the hope of moksha is not an excuse to neglect homework or to be cruel on the way. Dharma guides the other aims. That is why a stolen sweet is not a rightful enjoyment, and a profit made by cheating a classmate is not rightful artha.

### A story shape
Think of a market seller who gives correct measure and still earns a living. The seller has artha, but dharma decides the measure. Think of King Harishchandra, who would not drop truth to get his comfort back. Comfort is an aim. Truth is the guide.

### Your aims this term
You can want good marks (a kind of artha of effort), enjoy games (kama in a child's form), and still refuse to cheat (dharma). You can remember Paramatma at the end of the day (a step towards moksha, not a claim that you have finished the journey). Write your aims down. Cross out any aim that needs a lie.

## Key words
• Purushartha — the rightful aims of human life
• artha — material well-being and fairly earned wealth
• moksha — liberation; freedom from selfish bondage

studyPages.title: Lesson 3: Purushartha, the aims of life — Example 1
studyPages.body:
## Worked examples

### Example 1
Sort these aims: cheating to get money, playing a fair game, doing your class duty, remembering God. Which aim is not a rightful purushartha?

Working:
1. Class duty is dharma.
2. A fair game can be rightful enjoyment.
3. Remembering God looks towards moksha.
4. Cheating for money spoils artha because dharma is missing.

Answer: Cheating to get money is not a rightful aim.

## Activity: Four aims on a chart
You will need: A four-column chart

1. Head the columns Dharma, Artha, Kama and Moksha.

2. Under each, write one example that is right for a Grade 4 learner.

3. Cross-check the kama column so that it contains only proper joys, such as play or music.

4. Discuss how dharma guides the wish to have money.

## Practice

1. What is Purushartha?

2. Name the four aims.

3. Why is money earned by cheating not true artha?

## Answers to practice

1. The rightful aims of a human life.

2. Dharma, artha, kama and moksha.

3. Artha should be guided by dharma. Cheating breaks righteousness.

## Summary
• Purushartha includes dharma, artha, kama and moksha.
• Dharma must guide money and enjoyment.
• Children's rightful joys are things such as fair play, arts and family life, not harm.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Pranidaya, kindness to living beings — A story of refuge
studyPages.body:
LESSON 4: PRANIDAYA, KINDNESS TO LIVING BEINGS
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain Pranidaya as compassion for every living being.
• Apply it to animals, plants and people at school.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation; b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living

## Introduction
A living being does not have to be your friend before you refuse to harm it. Pranidaya joins two ideas: prani, a living being, and daya, mercy or compassion. It is kindness that notices life.

## Notes

### The meaning
The syllabus spells this principle Pranidaya. In this lesson it means daya, mercy, shown to every prani, every living being. People, animals and even the plants you studied as sacred are included. Compassion is not softness that ignores danger. You may step away from a snake and call an adult. You may not throw stones at the snake for fun.

### A story of refuge
A well-known moral story tells of King Shibi. A dove sought refuge with him, and a hawk demanded the dove as food. The king would not betray the bird that had trusted him. He offered his own flesh to match the dove's weight rather than break mercy. You are not asked to copy the injury. You are asked to copy the choice: a creature that comes to you for safety should not be handed to cruelty. In school, that may be a classmate hiding from bullies, or a bird that has fallen in the compound. Call an adult. Do not join the harm.

### Daily forms
- Do not hit animals or tear leaves off a living tree for sport.
- Share food with someone who has none, without making them feel small.
- Speak gently to a learner who is slow, afraid or new.
- If you keep a pet, give it water and do not neglect it.
- When you plant a seedling, you are also practising care for living things.

Peace in a class often begins with this principle. Cruel jokes are a failure of daya. A repaired friendship is a sign that mercy has done some work.

studyPages.title: Lesson 4: Pranidaya, kindness to living beings — Example 1
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• Pranidaya — compassion and mercy towards living beings
• daya — mercy or compassion
• prani — a living being

## Worked examples

### Example 1
Learners corner a frightened cat and laugh. Which principle is being broken, and what should a watcher do?

Working:
1. The cat is a prani. Cornering it for fun breaks Pranidaya.
2. The watcher should refuse to join in.
3. They should ask an adult to help the animal safely, not start a new attack.

Answer: Pranidaya is broken. Stop the teasing and get an adult to help.

## Activity: Skit of mercy
You will need: Space to act

1. In groups, act a short skit: a dove, or a classmate, asks for refuge, and the group chooses mercy instead of mockery.

2. Do not act injury. End with a safe, kind action.

3. Name the principle: Pranidaya.

4. Write one way you will show daya to a living being this week.

## Practice

1. What does Pranidaya mean in this lesson?

2. What choice does the story of King Shibi praise?

3. Give one way to practise Pranidaya at school.

## Answers to practice

1. Compassion or mercy shown to living beings.

2. He protected the dove that took refuge with him instead of giving it up to harm.

3. Any one: do not harm animals, do not mock a frightened classmate, speak gently, or care for a plant.

## Summary
• Pranidaya means mercy towards living beings.
• The story of King Shibi and the dove teaches refuge, not a dare to get hurt.
• School practice includes protecting animals and speaking kindly.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Punarjanam and the weight of actions
studyPages.body:
LESSON 5: PUNARJANAM AND THE WEIGHT OF ACTIONS
==============================================

## What you will learn
• Explain Punarjanam in simple, careful words.
• Show how good and harmful actions shape character now.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation; b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living

## Introduction
Punarjanam means birth again. Sanatan teaching says the soul does not finish its journey in a single lifetime, and that actions, called karma, matter. The point for a child is not to be frightened. The point is to choose good actions today.

## Notes

### The words
Punar means again. Janam means birth. Punarjanam is the teaching of rebirth. Karma means action, and also the moral weight actions carry. You are not asked to describe other people's past lives. You cannot see that, and guessing it is unkind. 'He is poor because of a past life' is a sentence this lesson forbids. It can be used to excuse meanness. Dharma tells you to help a person in need now.

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Punarjanam and the weight of actions — What you can know
studyPages.body:
### What you can know
You can know that habits grow. A learner who tells the truth finds it easier to tell the truth next time. A learner who mocks others becomes quicker to mock. Character is built, or spoiled, by repetition. Punarjanam extends that seriousness: Sanatan teaching says the soul carries the fruit of actions beyond what we can see in one term. Even if a classmate from another faith does not share the whole teaching, the shared moral is clear. What we do matters.

### Stories without scary detail
Scripture is full of people who met the fruit of pride and of people who were protected for their goodness. You already know Prahlad's faith and the fall of a cruel king. Use those stories to talk about justice and mercy, not to invent punishments for your enemies.

### Apply it
Before a harsh act, pause and ask: 'If this action shapes me, do I want that shape?' Then choose the kinder action. Apologise when you have been wrong, because repair is also karma of a good kind. Do not threaten a classmate with rebirth. That is bullying dressed up as religion.

Appreciate the principle as a call to responsibility. It makes ordinary kindness important.

## Key words
• Punarjanam — rebirth; the teaching that the soul is born again
• karma — action, and the moral result that actions bring

studyPages.title: Lesson 5: Punarjanam and the weight of actions — Answers to practice
studyPages.body:
## Worked examples

### Example 1
Someone says a classmate deserves unkindness because of punarjanam. What is the right reply?

Working:
1. You cannot know another person's unseen story.
2. Using the idea as an excuse to be cruel breaks dharma and Pranidaya.
3. The right use of the teaching is to watch your own actions.

Answer: Refuse the unkindness. Punarjanam is not a reason to hurt someone. It is a reason to choose good actions yourself.

## Activity: Actions that shape us
You will need: Two columns on paper

1. Head the columns 'Actions that build good character' and 'Actions that spoil it'.

2. List school examples in each column. Do not write classmates' names in the unkind column.

3. Discuss the meaning of Punarjanam without guessing anyone's past life.

4. Each learner writes one action they will repeat this week because it builds the character they want.

## Practice

1. What does Punarjanam mean?

2. What is karma in this lesson?

3. Why must you not blame a classmate's hardship on a past life?

## Answers to practice

1. Birth again; the teaching that the soul continues and is born again.

2. Action, and the moral weight or result that actions carry.

3. You cannot know that, and the idea must not be used to excuse unkindness. Dharma says to help.

## Summary
• Punarjanam means rebirth in Sanatan teaching.
• Karma means that actions matter and shape us.
• The teaching is not an excuse to be cruel or to guess another person's past.

LESSON 6: PRARTHANA, PRAYER THAT CHANGES THE DAY
================================================

## What you will learn
• Explain Prarthana as one of the five principles.
• Pray, or sit respectfully, in a way that includes thanks and a promise to do right.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation; b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living

## Introduction
You have already learned set prayers such as the Gayatri and Saraswati Vandana. Here prayer returns as a principle of dharma. Prarthana is not an extra hobby. It is one of the five supports of a righteous life.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Prarthana, prayer that changes the day — Manners
studyPages.body:
## Notes

### What this principle adds
Prarthana means prayer. As a principle of dharma it says that a good life stays in conversation with Paramatma. Prayer can thank, praise, ask for a clean heart, or admit a fault. Asking only for prizes, while refusing to change, is a thin kind of prayer.

A useful pattern for a child has three parts:
- **Thanks** — for parents, food, a new day, a friend
- **Sorry** — for a named fault, without hiding it
- **Please** — for courage to do one right action today

You may use the prayers of your own family. A learner from another home can sit quietly and respectfully while Sanatan classmates recite, and can still write the three-part pattern in their own words.

### Prayer and effort
Purushartha includes effort. Prarthana does not cancel effort. You pray, and you also revise. You pray, and you also apologise to the person you hurt. Scripture praises people who remembered God and then did the duty in front of them.

### Manners
Pray in a clean, quiet corner if you can. Do not shove. Do not laugh at a posture of prayer you do not use at home. If the class recites a prayer you have been taught, join sincerely or remain silent and still. Both can be respectful. Whispering jokes during a prayer breaks the principle you are studying.

The link with the other principles is simple. In prayer you turn to Paramatma, you ask for dharma to guide your aims, you ask for daya, and you ask for strength to choose good actions.

studyPages.title: Lesson 6: Prarthana, prayer that changes the day — A three-part prayer
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• Prarthana — prayer; speaking with God

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A learner prays to pass a test and then copies the answers. Which part of the principle was missed?

Working:
1. Prayer was used like a shortcut.
2. Dharma and honest purushartha were ignored.
3. A fitting prayer would ask for a clear mind and would be followed by real revision and honest writing.

Answer: The learner separated prayer from right action. Prayer should be followed by honest effort.

## Activity: A three-part prayer
You will need: Exercise book, A quiet moment

1. Write three lines beginning Thank you, I am sorry, and Please help me to do one right action.

2. If the class recites a known prayer such as the Gayatri or Saraswati Vandana, do so respectfully. Learners who do not recite sit quietly.

3. Share only the 'please' line if you want to, not a private 'sorry' that names other children.

4. Visit is not required today. If you later visit a mandir, remember this principle and observe the rites you have been taught.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Stories that carry the principles
studyPages.body:
## Practice

1. What is Prarthana?

2. Name the three parts of the simple prayer pattern in this lesson.

3. Why is praying and then cheating a failure of this principle?

## Answers to practice

1. Prayer.

2. Thanks, sorry, and please help me to do what is right.

3. Prarthana is meant to turn a person towards God and towards right action, not to excuse a wrong act.

## Summary
• Prarthana is prayer, one of the five principles.
• A simple pattern is thanks, sorry and a request for help to do right.
• Prayer works together with effort and honesty.

LESSON 7: STORIES THAT CARRY THE PRINCIPLES
===========================================

## What you will learn
• Match a moral story to the principle it teaches.
• Explain how stories build character when they are retold accurately.

Curriculum outcomes: a) identify five selected Principles of Dharma according to Sanatan/Vedic for familiarisation; c) appreciate the Principles of Dharma in building up one’s character

## Introduction
Principles can sound like a word list until a story gives them legs. Sanatan and Vedic tradition teaches through stories. The skill is to know which principle a story is carrying, and not to twist the story into something it did not say.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Stories that carry the principles — Matches you can defend
studyPages.body:
## Notes

### Matches you can defend
- **Prahlad and Narsimha** carry Paramatma: God is the one to worship, and God protects a faithful person. They also warn against pride.
- **A fair seller, or Harishchandra's love of truth**, carries Purushartha: rightful aims stay under dharma.
- **King Shibi and the dove** carries Pranidaya: mercy to a living being that seeks refuge.
- **The repeated truth about habits** carries Punarjanam carefully: actions shape a person, and Sanatan teaching says their weight continues. Do not add a made-up past life.
- **A child who prays and then does the chore** carries Prarthana joined to effort.

If you tell these stories in a skit, keep the match. A skit that turns Shibi into a bully has lost the principle. A skit that uses Punarjanam to mock a classmate has become cruel.

### Character
Character is what you are when the skit is over. Stories build it when you admire the right action and repeat a piece of it. They fail when you only enjoy the costume. Appreciation of the principles means you want a character that is reverent, fair, merciful, responsible and prayerful.

### At the mandir or at home
If you visit a Sanatan temple, you may see pictures of these stories on a wall. Ask a parent or priest what the picture teaches. Share the answer in class in your own words. Do not invent a label for a picture you do not know. A digital reading, if the teacher downloads a text, should be a source you can name, not a page of unkind comments.

studyPages.title: Lesson 7: Stories that carry the principles — Match stories to principles
studyPages.body:
## Key words
• character — the moral qualities that show what a person is really like

## Worked examples

### Example 1
A group acts King Shibi throwing the dove to the hawk, and they call it Pranidaya. What is wrong?

Working:
1. The story's mercy is the protection of the dove.
2. Throwing the dove away reverses the teaching.
3. The skit should be redone so that refuge is honoured.

Answer: The skit teaches the opposite of Pranidaya and should be corrected.

## Activity: Match stories to principles
You will need: Story cards, Principle cards

1. Match each story you have learned to Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam or Prarthana.

2. Perform one corrected skit that keeps the true lesson.

3. After the skit, say how the story could build character in your class.

4. Help a learner who needs the matching done orally.

## Practice

1. Which principle is taught by the story of King Shibi and the dove?

2. Which principle is clearest in Prahlad's refusal to worship a proud king as God?

3. How can a story build character rather than only entertain?

## Answers to practice

1. Pranidaya, compassion for a living being.

2. Paramatma.

3. When the listener copies the right action, such as telling the truth or showing mercy.

## Summary
• Each principle can be carried by a true story.
• A skit must not reverse mercy or invent someone's past life.
• Stories build character when the right action is copied in real life.

LESSON 8: BUILDING CHARACTER DAY BY DAY
=======================================

## What you will learn
• Apply all five principles to one school day.
• Explain why character is built by repeated choices.

Curriculum outcomes: b) apply the five selected Principles of Dharma in daily life for harmonious living; c) appreciate the Principles of Dharma in building up one’s character

## Introduction
Knowing five names is the start. A harmonious life is the aim. This lesson walks through one ordinary day and asks where Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam and Prarthana can actually appear.

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: Building character day by day — A day mapped to the five
studyPages.body:
## Notes

### A day mapped to the five
- **Morning prarthana:** thank Paramatma, and ask for a clean heart.
- **On the way to school:** show Pranidaya. Do not throw stones at animals. Help a smaller child cross safely if a known adult has asked you to walk together.
- **In class:** let dharma guide purushartha. Do your own work. Enjoy break without cheating at games.
- **When you are angry:** remember that actions shape you. A cruel reply is a seed you will meet again in your own habits. Choose repair instead.
- **Evening:** pray again, naming one good act and one act you will improve. That honesty is character under construction.

### Harmony
Harmonious living means people can share a room, a home and a road without fear of mockery or cheating. The five principles serve that peace. A class that prays and then bullies is not harmonious. A class that is kind but never tells the truth is not harmonious either. Dharma holds the pieces together.

### Appreciation
Write a short paragraph that begins, 'I appreciate these principles because...' Give a real reason: they stop you treating people as tools, they put money under honesty, they make prayer practical. Read it only if you wish. Appreciation that is copied from a neighbour without thought is thin.

studyPages.title: Lesson 8: Building character day by day — My five-principle day
studyPages.body:
### Keep going
Choose one principle that is weakest in you and one action for the next seven days. Tell a parent. If you fail on Tuesday, continue on Wednesday. Character is repetition, not a single perfect morning. When you next visit a mandir or sit with a grandparent, ask them which of the five they think a child should practise first, and listen.

## Key words
• harmonious — living together in fairness, peace and respect
• character — the kind of person your repeated choices are making

## Worked examples

### Example 1
During one afternoon a learner cheats in a game, laughs at a bird, and refuses to pray because 'principles are only for the exercise book'. Which principles need repair?

Working:
1. Cheating breaks dharma inside Purushartha.
2. Laughing at the bird breaks Pranidaya.
3. Refusing even a moment of respect breaks the daily place of Prarthana. All three can be repaired by an apology and a different choice.

Answer: Purushartha guided by dharma, Pranidaya and Prarthana.

## Activity: My five-principle day
You will need: Exercise book

1. Draw a simple day from morning to evening.

2. Write one action beside each of the five principles.

3. Share the plan in a group and correct any action that contradicts the principle.

4. Peer-teach the five names to a classmate who was away, using your day plan as the examples.

## Practice

1. Give one morning action and one class action that apply the principles.

2. Why is a single good morning not yet a full character?

3. How do the five principles help people live together harmoniously?

## Answers to practice

1. Morning: a short prayer of thanks. Class: doing your own work, or another true pair.

2. Character is built by repeating right choices, including starting again after a failure.

3. They teach reverence, fair aims, mercy, responsibility for actions and prayer, which reduce bullying and cheating.

## Summary
• Each part of the day can carry one of the five principles.
• Harmony needs honesty and kindness together.
• Character grows when a chosen action is repeated, including after a failure.

studyPages.title: Revision quiz
studyPages.body:
REVISION QUIZ
=============

Answer all the questions, then mark yourself on the Answers tab.

1. Which list is the five principles of this sub-strand?
   A. Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam, Prarthana
   B. Bhastrika, Vajrasana, Ganga, Tulsi, Rama
   C. Monday to Friday only
   D. Four aims without Paramatma

2. Paramatma means
   A. A type of food
   B. The Supreme Soul, God
   C. A passenger fare
   D. A yoga mat

3. The four aims inside Purushartha are
   A. Dharma, artha, kama and moksha
   B. Four rivers
   C. Four festivals
   D. Four postures

4. Money gained by cheating fails Purushartha because
   A. Money is always evil
   B. Artha must be guided by dharma
   C. Children may not count coins
   D. Prayer forbids all work

5. Pranidaya in this lesson means
   A. Compassion towards living beings
   B. A fierce breath
   C. Rebirth
   D. A tower on a mandir

6. King Shibi and the dove teach learners to
   A. Hand a frightened creature to harm
   B. Protect a living being that seeks refuge
   C. Ignore all animals
   D. Win by cheating

7. A careful way to speak about Punarjanam is
   A. Guess a classmate's past life and mock them
   B. Say that actions matter and that the teaching is about responsibility, not an excuse to be cruel
   C. Claim you remember everyone's former birth
   D. Use it as a swear word

8. Prarthana is applied best when a learner
   A. Prays and then cheats
   B. Prays with thanks and also does the honest work
   C. Mocks people who pray
   D. Shouts over a prayer

9. How do these principles build character?

10. Which action shows appreciation of the principles in daily life?
   A. Bullying after a prayer
   B. Doing your own work, showing mercy to an animal, and praying honestly
   C. Inventing a past life for a rival
   D. Using holy names as jokes

studyPages.title: Quiz answers
studyPages.body:
ANSWERS
=======

1. A. Paramatma, Purushartha, Pranidaya, Punarjanam, Prarthana
   The design names these five Sanatan or Vedic principles.

2. B. The Supreme Soul, God
   Parama means supreme and atma means soul.

3. A. Dharma, artha, kama and moksha
   Purushartha gathers these rightful aims, with dharma as the guide.

4. B. Artha must be guided by dharma
   Rightful wealth stays under righteousness.

5. A. Compassion towards living beings
   It is daya, mercy, towards every prani, every living being.

6. B. Protect a living being that seeks refuge
   The story is used to teach Pranidaya, not violence.

7. B. Say that actions matter and that the teaching is about responsibility, not an excuse to be cruel
   The principle calls for responsibility. It must not become bullying.

8. B. Prays with thanks and also does the honest work
   Prayer and right effort belong together.

9. They train repeated choices of reverence, fairness, mercy, responsibility and prayer until those choices become the kind of person you are.
   Character is built by practice, not by a list left in a book.

10. B. Doing your own work, showing mercy to an animal, and praying honestly
   Appreciation is visible in harmonious, truthful behaviour.
